name: Meadow
lede: Meadow is a dark, slightly yellowish green named for hay-and-grass country, a word that mineralogists, pigment makers and painters each used in their own way.

sections.title: A word for a place
sections.body:
*Meadow* names a place before it names a color, and the books that mention the color are mostly describing the place. Pastoureau notes that Roman writers such as Virgil praised [[green]] because it dominates meadows, woods and gardens and rests the eye [1]. In the age of Saint Louis, he adds, green counted as a cool color and blue as a warm one, the reverse of today's habit [1].

In the romances and pageantry of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries the meadow had a fixed role. The ideal orchard garden had at its center the *prael*, a small meadow of lawn and flowers around a fountain [2]. Tournaments were held in the open, at the edge of a forest or on a wide meadow, and the stands were hung with green cloth [3]. Pastoureau follows the same ground forward to the card table: the green meadow of ordeals and tournaments, the green baize of games and the modern sports field all carry the idea that fate is decided on green [4].

sections.title: The swatch and the word
sections.body: The swatch is a deep, shaded green, filed in Maerz and Paul's *Dictionary of Color* of 1930 as plate 30, block D10 [15]. Its nearest ISCC-NBS 1955 name is dark yellowish green (block 137), at a CIEDE2000 distance of 4.8 [15]. It is the green of a meadow edge under a hedge rather than of grass in full sun; the lighter greens are [[grass-green]] and [[apple-green]]. Do not confuse it with [[mountain-meadow]], a bright blue-green that comes from a different list [15].

sections.title: In the mineralogists' lists
sections.body:
Before it was a paint chip, meadow green was a term in mineralogy. In 1774 Abraham Gottlob Werner published a list of 54 color names for describing minerals, and his students and translators kept extending it [8]. Richard Kirwan, working from Claudine Picardet's French version, added sparrow-grass green and copper yellow in 1794, and Baty calls it debatable whether sparrow-grass green meant the same as grass green or what Kirwan implied by meadow green [8].

Meadow green sits between emerald and apple green in several Werner-descended lists that Baty reproduces [9]. It does not appear among the greens of the Syme list of 1814 or the Cleaveland list of 1816 that he prints, which run from verdigris and celadon through emerald and apple to [[pistachio]] and olive [9]. The name belonged to the earlier, looser vocabulary and did not survive into the standard chart.

sections.title: Meadow green as a pigment
sections.body:
Meadow green was also a trade name. The *Pigment Compendium* lists it as the English form of the German *Wiesengrün*, which Rose in 1916 described as a mixture of copper arsenite, copper phosphate and copper carbonate [10]. The same pages list May green as an uncommon name for [[emerald-green]], probably marking a shade variant [10]. The name stood for a shade, not for one substance.

The older meadow greens came from plants. Ball groups iris green, made from the juice of iris flowers with water and possibly alum, together with folium and weld as colors of the meadow, not the mine [18]. A monk could gather them himself, as the medieval writer Heraclius advises [18].

sections.title: Meadows in the eye of painters and critics
sections.body:
Gage traces an old comparison between a church floor of colored marble and a flowery meadow, an image with a Classical pedigree [5]. Birren, in an older survey, reports that Egyptian temple floors were often painted green like the meadows of the Nile [14]. Finlay records that the gem writer Thomas Nicols claimed in 1692 that an [[gem:emerald|emerald]] seen beside a pleasant green meadow looked lovelier than the meadow [19].

Leonardo noticed that a figure standing on a meadow has the folds of its drapery tinged with the green reflected from the ground. Gage says it reads like a Renoir of the 1870s, but that Leonardo raised it mainly to set such effects aside in favor of an object's own color [6].

Old landscapes can mislead. Pastoureau warns that the impression of dark, autumnal countryside in earlier painting is a distorted view, created by greens that have browned and blues that have faded, and that skilled restoration has not repaired it [11]. Nor did Romanticism simply invent the love of greenery: from the later eighteenth century walks in meadows and woods became fashionable, but Pastoureau finds that green was not an especially emblematic Romantic color [12]. In the other direction, Gage reports that the Munich scientist Arnold Brass, a defender of Goethe's color theory, attacked the "violet meadows" of modern art [7].

sections.title: A dye works on a meadow
sections.body: The factory that made Perkin's [[mauve]] stood on a meadow [13]. Perkin and Sons settled on a little over six acres beside the Grand Junction Canal at Greenford Green, near Harrow, a site Garfield calls a modest place from which to plan a revolution in color [13]. The meadow often flooded when the nearby brook burst its banks, but the water supply was good and the canal could carry barges [13].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
These are our own measurements, from photographs of aged, varnished paintings; a color match is not a pigment test [16]. Within a CIEDE2000 distance of 6, and covering at least 5 percent of the canvas, this green appears in 46 of 23,781 paintings, about 1 in 500 [16].

The distribution is lopsided: 27 of the 46 are from the 1800s and 16 from the 1900s, and none is earlier than 1600 [16]. In the 1900s it turns up in 1.0 percent of the archive's 1,674 paintings, nearly five times the expected rate [16]. The earliest is Jan Brueghel the Elder's *Wooded Landscape with Travelers* of 1610, which our data dates 320 years before the color's first record in our sources [16][15]. The thin early archive and aged varnish make that a floor, not a first, and Pastoureau's warning about browned greens may explain part of the gap [11][16].

Four painters stand out. [[painter:paul-gauguin|Gauguin]] has it in 5 of his 50 works here, Van Gogh in 4 of 49, Vallotton in 3 of 40 and [[painter:auguste-renoir|Renoir]] in 3 of 46 [16]. Four of the 45 Post-Impressionist works in the archive carry it [16]. The largest area is in [[painting:commons-Q76627696|Gauguin's Still Life of 1899]], where it covers about 45 percent of the canvas [16]. In printed English the word *meadow* peaks in the 1800s, counting every sense, so that curve follows the landscape and not the color [17].

questions.q: Why can an old landscape painting give the false impression that its painter preferred dark, autumn colors?
choices: Greens in old paintings have browned and blues have faded
Painters before 1800 could not mix green
Meadows were painted brown by custom
questions.answer: Greens in old paintings have browned and blues have faded

questions.q: What did the pigment name meadow green (German Wiesengrün) describe in Rose's 1916 account?
choices: A mixture of copper arsenite, copper phosphate and copper carbonate
A blend of woad and weld
questions.answer: A mixture of copper arsenite, copper phosphate and copper carbonate
